precepts.why:
“Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, neither shalt thou mar the corners of thy beard.” It was not the custom of Israel to cut the beard, and that is why the shaving was so shameful.

David meant to show kindness to Hanun, because Nahash his father had shown kindness to David. But the princes of Ammon poisoned Hanun's mind, telling him David's comforters were come “to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land”, though that was not the case. So Hanun took David's servants “and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away.”

The men “were greatly ashamed” because they knew how to carry themselves as men of the Most High. Our ancestors had far more respect for themselves than to be exposed this way. So the king said, “Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.”

note.label: 1 Chronicles 19: War With Ammon and Syria

precepts.why:
“Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the Lord do that which is good in his sight.”

Joab spoke this with the battle set against him before and behind. The Ammonites had made themselves odious to David and hired thirty and two thousand chariots, with the king of Maachah and his people. So Joab divided the army: he took the choice of Israel against the Syrians and gave the rest to Abishai his brother against Ammon, saying, “If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee.”

Be of good courage, behave valiantly for the people and the cities of our God, and let the Most High do what is good in His sight. And He did: the Syrians fled before Joab, and when Ammon saw the Syrians flee, “they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city.”
